                                     PROJECT NO. 58000
 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                            §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                        §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                      §
 IN THE ERCOT REGION 9                           §                    OF TEXAS

     TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS’ COMMENTS TO PROPOSED
            AMENDMENTS TO §25.192 AND §25.193 AND NEW §25.252

                                      I.   INTRODUCTION

       This project will have profound consequences for the business community in Texas. For

industrial customers, electricity costs and regulatory stability are a driving factor in choosing

Texas. Substantial investment over more than twenty years has been predicated on a predictable

regulatory climate and settled rate policies that are being reopened in this rulemaking. Texas

Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) recognizes that it is time to revisit certain allocation policies

that have not been modified as the world has evolved—such as the four-coincident peak (4CP)

methodology and regularly updating class allocations for retail Transmission Cost Recovery

Factors (TCRFs). Yet, it is imperative that the Commission adopt durable, principled rules that

are not based on a particular development trend or moment in time. This state’s economy has been

built on a foundation of sound, cost-based rates, which equitably balances affordability for

residential and small commercial customers against fair, stable rates for the business community.

TIEC urges the Commission not to stray from this approach, which has set Texas apart in

competing for industrial and manufacturing projects that bring tax revenue, high-quality jobs, and

economic prosperity to the state.

       The proposed rule is applicable to all new large load customers over 75 MW, but it is no

secret that a driving political force behind these changes is the emergence of new, large




                                                 1
 computational loads.1 TIEC represents traditional industrial and manufacturing facilities, and the

Commission’s proposed framework presents significant and in some respects unworkable

challenges when applied to the industrial community. TIEC has engaged throughout the Senate

Bill 6 (SB 6) rulemakings to offer workable refinements (including proposing and supporting a

minimum transmission rate).2 At this time, however, TIEC remains concerned that the overall

approach reflected in the proposal is not well-suited to the realities of industrial operations, both

current and future.

            While TIEC has sought to avoid rate classifications driven by end-use of electricity or

business sector, there are significant differences in the development patterns of traditional

industrial loads and the new computational projects. As compared to traditional industrial projects,

data center loads are generally larger, more modular, and more operationally homogenous. They

typically have fewer siting needs and more aggressive energization timelines, with access to

electricity being the primary driver in both timing and location. Unlike data center loads, industrial

manufacturing facilities typically require highly specialized feedstocks, a long-term skilled

workforce (not just short-term construction), access to specific modes of transporting product to

global markets, and additional environmental specifications. These projects are developed often

over five-plus years and expanded over decades, representing massive, long-term investments that

 are not easily built, relocated, or decommissioned. This basic disparity in development and

operational horizons renders certain aspects of the proposed rules—particularly those tied to

aggressive minimum billing demands and long-term commitments calibrated to rapid ramp-up

assumptions, large demand projections, and a nascent industry sector—unnecessary and

unworkable for the industrial community.

       Many of the changes proposed in this rule will have potentially dramatic impacts on

traditional industrial customers, including altering the underlying economics of investment

decisions that have been made in the past. While TIEC understands the desire to revisit long-

standing practices, the Commission should remain open to mitigating these impacts or phasing in

the changes, particularly in cases where the outcomes would be extreme. For most TIEC members,

electricity is one of the top costs of production. TIEC’s member companies operate in competitive

global markets where prices are dictated by supply and demand, and major increases in electricity

costs often cannot just be passed through to its customers. As such, the Commission should be

mindful that massive cost increases for these businesses can create extreme economic challenges

for existing plants. These are important considerations that the Commission should keep in mind

as it deliberates on these proposed changes.

       With this context, TIEC has responded to Commission Staff’s questions and proposed a

number of specific adjustments, discussed in detail below, intended to make the proposed rules

administrable and more appropriately tailored for industrial manufacturers while preserving the

Commission’s underlying cost-recovery and reliability objectives.




                                               3
                           II.    RESPONSES TO STAFF’S QUESTIONS

1.      Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
        be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
        different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

        Load size would be a reasonable, non-discriminatory basis for establishing a large load

minimum billing demand.          Specifically, TIEC recommends a threshold for the minimum

transmission rate of 300 MW or more of incremental load requested within any three-year period

at a single location. While TIEC believes Staff’s intent is for this rule to only apply to new or

expanded interconnections, TIEC would recommend making that clear in this rule, as well as in

the pending rule in Project No. 58481. Notably, the proposed definition of “large load customer”

in Project No. 58481 is problematic because it keys in on the customer’s “total expected non-

coincident peak demand at a single site,” which would subject an existing customer’s entire load

to the minimum rate whenever any expansion pushes total site demand to 75 MW or above—even

if the incremental addition itself is small. In particular, the rule should be clear that if a site pursues

an expansion, the pre-existing portion of the site will not be subject to the minimum demand charge

as a result of that expansion.

        To avoid this overbroad reading, we propose that the definition of Large Load Customer

in Project No. 58481 (which is used in this rulemaking) be revised to clarify that the 75 MW

threshold is measured against the incremental load being added, rather than the customer’s total

existing site demand. Correspondingly, TIEC’s related redlines in Attachment A to this rule

should be read to apply only to incremental load.

        As noted above, the impetus for this new minimum rate construct appears to be concerns

about the significant transmission needs for a high volume of “extra” large loads. It is not being

driven by the steady, incremental industrial development that the state has successfully managed

                                                    4
 for decades. In general, a 300 MW threshold appears to provide a reasonable distinction between

historical projects and these new “extra-fast and extra-large projects” that are driving the minimum

rate policy. Very few traditional industrial customers exceed 300 MW at a single location, and

those that do typically developed the projects in phases over many years that were each under 300

MW. TIEC acknowledges that it recommended a 250 MW threshold in prior comments on this

topic, which was based on the actual operational loads for legacy industrial businesses. However,

after further diligence TIEC has concluded that the interconnection requests/non-coincident peaks

are often slightly oversized for all customers for contingency scenarios (this is discussed further

below). Recognizing this dynamic, TIEC is adjusting its recommendation to 300 MW and above

to provide an additional buffer.

       For the historical cadence of new sub-300 MW industrial loads, the existing

interconnection   framework—including        financial   security,   ramping   requirements,    and

contributions-in-aid-of-construction (CIAC)—has worked well for decades, allowing meaningful

protections against shifting costs to other customers without imposing unmanageable up-front

financial burdens on companies seeking to do business in Texas.

       Notably, however, a 300 MW threshold will still capture certain types of industrial

projects—including those that are critical to state and national priorities. Specifically, LNG

facilities and semiconductor fabrication plants are still likely to be picked up by this threshold.

The state competes heavily to attract these businesses, which often represent tens of billions in

long-term investment. Hefty up-front minimum transmission rate requirements imposed before a

project is fully operational could be a major deterrent. Legislators have repeatedly raised concerns

about ensuring that requirements aimed at data centers do not stop traditional businesses from



                                                 5
 siting in Texas.3 Applying the same undifferentiated minimum billing demand requirements to

these industries will risk disadvantaging Texas when these customers are deciding where to locate

their next facility or whether or not to expand. The Commission should consider an exemption

process or alternative path for these types of projects. Alternatively, while it is not TIEC’s

preferred approach, the Commission may ultimately need to consider distinguishing between

computational loads and traditional industrial loads if it seeks to pursue policies that are not

manageable for the industrial community. This is discussed further below.

        Finally, TIEC recognizes that there will be an incentive to “game” the threshold by

building, for example, 299.9 MW loads. TIEC believes this concern can be addressed without

abandoning a size-based threshold based on current development trends, where market demand is

predominantly for sites with 500, 1000, or 2000 MW of demand. Given that this emerging market

does not appear to be as cost-sensitive, it is likely that the demand for a larger site will outweigh

the cost consequences of exceeding the threshold for a minimum transmission rate. Further, the

Commission could apply the 300 MW threshold to a customer whose contracted peak demand or

non-coincident peak demand reaches 300 MW in the aggregate over a rolling three-year period,

whether through a single interconnection or several related interconnections. A rolling three-year

test would prevent a customer from avoiding the minimum billing demand simply by phasing an

expansion into sub-300 MW increments that, together, add up to a single large load addition.

        In Attachment A to these comments, TIEC has provided alternative redlines to implement

a threshold of 300 MW or more of new incremental load, as measured on a three-year basis, as

well as an alternative computational load approach. Under the 300 MW option, TIEC has also


        3
           See GridMonitor, Senate Committee on Business and Commerce at 3:46:53 -3:47:21 (April 1, 2026)
(available at: https://dash2.gridmonitor.com/sharing/?token=***                                                   6
 provided a process to request a good cause exception where (a) the minimum billing demand will

create an undue financial hardship on the large load customer and (b) the overall value of the large

load to the state, considering factors such as job creation, tax revenues, long-term financial

commitments, site-specific fixed capital investment, long-term operating permits, and other proof

of long-term financial commitment to operating at the site, outweighs the need for a minimum

billing demand.

2.      Should the large load minimum billing demand be: fixed for 20 years as proposed;
        reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or extended to a longer time period?

        A shorter, fixed term of approximately five years is appropriate for traditional industrial

customers, and any phase-down should be built around that shorter horizon rather than stretched

across twenty years. For the cadence and size of traditional industrial growth, there is very limited

risk of any “stranded” facilities or cost-shifting. Typically, any theoretically under-utilized

capacity on the system is either: (a) covered by existing CIAC and/or financial security

requirements, if the facilities are driven by the individual customer, or (b) fully utilized by other

customers within five years or less for more general system upgrades.

        The proposed rule would require a large load customer to begin 20 years of billing as soon

as service is available, regardless of whether the customer has energized or is using its full capacity.

While the rule does not address this, in other jurisdictions these types of minimum rates have come

along with collateral/security requirements. TIEC would expect the utilities to impose these

requirements if they are not addressed in the rule. The longer this minimum billing demand period

runs, the longer a customer’s collateral and security obligations must remain in place to support it,

and the amounts of security being held will be orders of magnitude higher than what utilities have




                                                   7
 typically had to manage.4 Lengthening the minimum commitment period beyond what ratepayer

protection requires would increase collateral requirements and deter economic development. For

cost-sensitive traditional manufacturing customers, a 20-year minimum billing demand—paired

with the security and CIAC obligations under development in Project No. 58481—is simply

unworkable.

           Importantly, TIEC’s members make long-term investments and rarely shut them down

within decades of their construction. The infrastructure required for complex industrial facilities

is capital-intensive and site-specific, and it typically takes years to plan, permit, and construct.

Texas utilities have extensive experience in planning for and interacting with these customers.

Because of this, the risk that a traditional industrial load will fail to materialize or will abandon its

capacity after interconnecting is fundamentally different from the risk that the large load minimum

billing demand provisions appear to be designed to address. As noted above, based on historical

load growth, any theoretically underutilized system upgrades would likely be used by other

customers within a five-year growth period, and stakeholders have broadly agreed with that

timeframe.5 A minimum billing demand period that runs four times that length is not calibrated to

the actual risk presented by traditional industrial loads. A five-year term also gives ERCOT and

the relevant TSP enough historical demand data to accurately forecast a large load’s expected

contribution to coincident peak demand going forward and factor that into future forecasts, which

demand.

           While other jurisdictions have adopted some longer-term commitments,6 these appear to

be premised on hyperscale data centers and other large computational loads that those jurisdictions

fear may relocate, restructure, or abandon requested capacity as their business needs or site

selection evolve. They are also often implemented in customer-specific special rates, rather than

a general rule for all customers over a certain size. TIEC does not take a position on whether a

longer commitment term is the right answer for that type of load (noting the potential difficulties

it creates). But applying that same extended term to traditional industrial customers, whose

operational history and profiles are known, would have unintended consequences and is not

necessary to protect the system from the risks created by traditional industrial development.

           TIEC shares the Commission’s interest in protecting ratepayers from cost-shifting and from

paying for capacity that a large load reserves but never uses. At the same time, the Commission

should be mindful that a minimum billing demand period set longer than necessary does not

meaningfully improve ratepayer protection—it simply imposes additional, unnecessary cost and

minimum billing demand period, set at approximately five years for traditional industrial loads

that protects against cost-shifting without making it commercially impractical for businesses to

develop projects in Texas.

       In Attachment A, TIEC has provided suggested changes to modify the term of the

minimum rate to five years in § 25.193(d)(3) and 25.252(e)(2)(ii).

3.     Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
       lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
       load minimum billing demand:
       a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
           is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
           demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in
           phases over the years, and how?
       b.   be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
            load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
            customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
            year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand?
       If so, should the percentage weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP
       demand decline in phases over the years, and how?
       As applied to industrial loads, the minimum demand should: (a) be based on a percentage

of contract demand or, if higher, the customer’s actual non-coincident peak in a given year, and

(b) track the ramp submitted by the customer, and not penalize an individual customer if the utility

builds out system upgrades ahead of the customer’s needs based on economies of scale,

construction efficiency, etc. This will protect against cost-shifting and stranded costs while

treating large customers equitably with all other customers and reflecting how the system is

actually planned.

       Using 100% minimum billing demand is unreasonable for traditional industrial loads and

would treat large customers unfairly as compared to other customer classes. Both the transmission



                                                10
 and distribution systems must be built to withstand contingencies, including the highest possible

load (the “non-coincident peak”) of all customers on the system or a portion of the system

occurring at once. For the transmission system, this is reflected in planning for a system-wide

demand that sums the non-coincident peaks of all the individual weather zones. On the distribution

system, it is driven by projecting NCPs for individual customers served by different distribution

elements, which are sized for local needs. In either case, utilities typically estimate demand for all

customers, in all classes with an additional buffer relative to expected operations to ensure

reliable service during these contingency peak scenarios. So, for example, the interconnection for

a residential customer might be based on what is needed for the customer to run its air conditioning

unit, pool pump, electric dryer and all the lighting in the house when it is 105 degrees outside.

However, residential customers typically do not reach these demand levels, and their billing is

based on actual usage/demand, not projections used for interconnection sizing and system

planning. Similarly, industrial interconnections must be designed for a plant to run all of its

energy-intensive processes at the same time during extreme weather, but it is not expected that this

will routinely occur nor should the industrial customer be billed based on this presumption.

       For large loads, TIEC submits that a reasonable minimum billing demand standard would

be based on 75%-80% of the large load customer’s contracted peak demand, or its actual NCP

demand in a given year if higher than this percentage. This reflects the dynamic described above




                                                 11
 and is consistent with the approach adopted in other jurisdictions.7 Notably, Texas Energy Buyer’s

Alliance (TEBA) commissioned an independent study to evaluate the minimum billing demand

level necessary to ensure transmission investments made to serve new large loads do not shift costs

to customers under a 12CP methodology.8 That study found that a minimum billing demand level

of 75% of contracted demand is approximately rate-neutral for existing residential customers, and

that a minimum billing demand of 80% is projected to reduce transmission rates for existing

residential customers relative to the base case.9 This aligns with TIEC’s estimate of the appropriate

minimum percentage threshold.

           Alternatively, a standard based on some portion of the customer’s historical NCP demand,

rather than its full contracted demand, would also be workable and may better reflect a load’s

demonstrated system impact over time. However, this would generally be lower than a percentage

of contract demand. Under either approach, caution must be taken not to create an incentive for

 customers to undersize their facilities relative to their actual anticipated needs. If the minimum

billing demand is calculated as a high percentage of a contracted amount that a customer

deliberately sets too low, that under-sizing could compromise reliability by leaving inadequate

capacity margin for the load's actual operations. Any threshold the Commission adopts should be

paired with safeguards to ensure that contracted demand figures remain an honest representation

of a customer’s anticipated need, not a number gamed downward to minimize billing exposure.

       Under all scenarios, an industrial customer’s minimum billing demand should be tied to

the ramp they submitted and not the capacity available to them at a given time based on utility

construction and planning preferences. TIEC members are willing to be held to their submitted

ramps, but if it makes more sense based on economies of scale, construction realities, regulatory

considerations, or other factors for a utility to build out capacity ahead of the customer’s needs

then the customer should not be required to start paying for this capacity before they said it would

be needed. For industrial businesses, this is necessary to align rates with increased revenue streams

as a facility ramps over time. Requiring a customer to pay rates based on the full available capacity

prior to needing it is unjust and is not how other customers are treated in other classes.

       Importantly, utilities often build out direct interconnection facilities to meet a customer’s

end-use demand, but large customers pay for this directly through CIAC.                      All direct

interconnection costs—including substations and other facilities dedicated to a specific large

load—are already paid for directly by that customer through contributions in aid of construction

and financial security requirements. The minimum billing demand discussion in this proceeding

concerns only the broader transmission infrastructure that also serves all other customers on the

system. Utilities generally should use customers’ ramps for planning purposes and not the end-

use demand at some future point, so it is clear there are not any costs being shifted or stranded.

                                                 13
 That shared-use character supports tracking a load’s actual materialization over time, rather than

locking in a fixed billing obligation for 20 years. Even though transmission facilities may be built

out in response to a particular large load’s request, those facilities do not serve that load

exclusively—they become part of the interconnected system used by all customers. ERCOT

should track and evaluate a load’s actual demand and materialization on an ongoing basis, and

after a few years of operational data—including situations where the customer has added co-

generation and has limited grid withdrawals—that data should be incorporated directly into

ERCOT’s planning models. If a load is not materializing as originally projected, transmission

upgrades should not continue to be planned or built out indefinitely to serve demand that the data

shows is not actually there.

       In Attachment A, TIEC has suggested proposed rule language in § 25.193(d)(2) and

§ 25.252(e)(2)(ii) make the minimum rate the greater (i) of 75% of the customer’s submitted ramp

rate, whether or not the customer is energized or achieving that ramp, or (ii) the customer’s actual

demand during any given 12CP interval.

4.     Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as
       an entity that is subject to § 25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
       Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
       electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and
       cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include
       applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large
       computational loads.

       PURA § 36.003 requires rates to be just and reasonable, and not unreasonably preferential,

prejudicial, or discriminatory, and sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each class

of consumer.10      Essentially, this provision prohibits treating similarly situated customers



      10
           PURA § 36.003.

                                                 14
 differently but does not prohibit drawing reasonable distinctions among customer classes that may

have different usage patterns, operational characteristics, or other common features.                               The

Commission has long recognized that differential treatment among classes is allowed under certain

circumstances—where there is a reasoned justification for the distinctions being created. As stated

recently in Docket No. 59009 regarding retail transmission rates, “[differential treatment] is often

inherent in rates based on reasonable justification.”11

         Texas courts have long confirmed that PURA §36.003 (including its predecessor PURA

§38) does not mandate uniform rates across all customers; rather, it prohibits only unreasonable

discrimination.12 Where the Commission sets different rates for customers who might otherwise

appear similarly situated, the disparate treatment must be grounded in “substantial and reasonable

differences” between the customer groups.13 The factors that may justify such distinctions are

broad, including the quantity of service received, the different characteristics of service, the time

of use, the cost of service, the constancy and regularity of use, “or any other matter which presents

a substantial difference as a ground of distinction.”14 Importantly, the burden of proving that a

rate classification is unreasonably discriminatory falls on the party challenging the classification,

5.     Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
       serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       The definition of transmission interconnection costs should not be broadened to include

transmission projects recommended at the conclusion of a batch study.            The fundamental

distinction in transmission cost recovery is between costs dedicated to serving a specific customer

and costs that benefit the broader system. Costs dedicated to a specific customer should be

recovered through a CIAC— a direct, upfront payment from that customer—rather than socialized

into transmission rates paid by all ratepayers. Only costs that serve the system as a whole belong

in rates. Broadening the interconnection-cost definition to sweep in system upgrades identified by




                                                 18
 the batch process risks blurring this line and improperly shifts system-level costs needed to serve

both existing and new customers onto individual new customers.

       ERCOT’s batch process analyzes transmission needs for all loads seeking interconnection

through the Batch process along with all existing load. The system must be designed and built to

serve all customers, and if existing customers did not exist, a different set of upgrades would be

identified. Further, it is impossible to identify which particular system upgrades are attributable

to an individual customer. Transmission planning studies model all existing and planned load

under various contingencies, and identified upgrades may be driven by locational constraints and

specific contingency assumptions rather than the general usage of a particular customer or group

of customers. It is not possible to isolate what portion of the resulting transmission investment is

“caused” by any single customer or individual load. It is therefore inappropriate—and technically

infeasible—to treat batch-study-driven project costs as interconnection costs that can be directly

assigned to a specific customer.

6.     If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
       whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
       how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
       and transmission planning studies?

       This question raises a complicated and important issue as to whether a minimum

transmission rate should allow a customer to reserve transmission capacity for the duration of the

minimum rate. While TIEC understands the Commission wants to protect against cost-shifting,

the reality is that requiring or allowing customers to reserve capacity that they are not using by

paying a minimum transmission rate is not good for the state’s growth and will have substantial

unintended consequences. Even if capacity is being paid for through a minimum charge, reserved

but unused capacity sits unproductive and does not fuel the state’s economy. Warehousing


                                                19
 capacity in this way ties up valuable infrastructure without producing any of the economic benefits

the state is otherwise trying to capture from large load growth. In fact, it likely impedes growth

by resulting in more protracted interconnection timelines for other customers who want to actually

operate—such as traditional industrial businesses. Reserved but unused capacity does not generate

the revenue, tax dollars, or jobs that would flow from actual load utilization. For this reason,

reserving capacity for extended periods without use should not be permitted. A maximum

reservation period of two to three years represents a reasonable outer limit.

       However, if reserved capacity is reclaimed or reallocated because the customer has not

used it within the applicable time limit, it would be inequitable to continue holding that customer

to the full minimum charge associated with that capacity (as well as any related security). Any

minimum billing demand or minimum charge obligation should be adjusted downward in

proportion to the amount of capacity actually reclaimed/reallocated. A customer should not be

able to retain capacity for an extended period through paying a minimum rate, but also should be

billed only for the capacity actually available to it. Notably, a five-year minimum rate term would

alleviate this issue by limiting the period a customer can hold unused capacity and also limiting

the period where a customer would be charged for capacity they are not using to five years.

       If capacity can be held under a minimum rate, this creates additional planning challenges

and the potential for additional underutilized infrastructure. Resource adequacy reports and

assessments should not be inflated by counting reserved but unused capacity as if it were being

used. For resource adequacy, projections should be based on the site’s actual historical usage,

perhaps with some adjustment based on historical growth trends, but not the customer’s theoretical

or contracted reservation level. This would produce a distorted and misleading picture of system



                                                20
 reliability and resource needs. Accurate resource adequacy reporting depends on real, verified

usage data rather than paper reservations.

       However, transmission planning studies present a different consideration. Transmission

planning models would still need to continue reflecting this capacity as used, otherwise it would

not actually be reserved. If a customer is permitted to reserve capacity, transmission planning

must reflect that reservation for so long as it is being held. Otherwise, the infrastructure necessary

to serve that load when it materializes will not be available, and the customer’s expectation and

the capacity it paid for will not be honored. This highlights why long-term capacity reservations

are inefficient, costly, and not good policy. TIEC continues to urge that a five-year minimum rate

and corresponding reservation right would be a reasonable way to address these issues.

       In Attachment A, TIEC has proposed changes to § 25.252 to: (a) clarify that the

interconnection agreement term and minimum billing demand requirements only apply to

customers subject to the minimum billing demand feature under § 25.193(d) or who opt-in to

reserve capacity, not all large customers, (b) provide that if capacity is reallocated, the minimum

billing demand construct will also be terminated for that capacity, and (c) specify that capacity can

customer is paying minimum billing demand on such capacity. TIEC also added a reference to

optional capacity reservations in § 25.192(b) to ensure that billing demand from customers who

                                      I.   INTRODUCTION

       This project will have profound consequences for the business community in Texas. For

industrial customers, electricity costs and regulatory stability are a driving factor in choosing

Texas. Substantial investment over more than twenty years has been predicated on a predictable

regulatory climate and settled rate policies that are being reopened in this rulemaking. Texas

Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) recognizes that it is time to revisit certain allocation policies

that have not been modified as the world has evolved-such as the four-coincident peak (4CP)

methodology and regularly updating class allocations for retail Transmission Cost Recovery

Factors (TCRFs). Yet, it is imperative that the Commission adopt durable, principled rules that

are not based on a particular development trend or moment in time. This state' s economy has been

built on a foundation of sound, cost-based rates, which equitably balances affordability for

residential and small commercial customers against fair, stable rates for the business community.

TIEC urges the Commission not to stray from this approach, which has set Texas apart in

competing for industrial and manufacturing projects that bring tax revenue, high-quality jobs, and

economic prosperity to the state.

       The proposed rule is applicable to all new large load customers over 75 MW, but it is no

secret that a driving political force behind these changes is the emergence of new, large




                                                 1
 computational loads. 1 TIEC represents traditional industrial and manufacturing facilities, and the

Commission' s proposed framework presents significant and in some respects unworkable

challenges when applied to the industrial community. TIEC has engaged throughout the Senate

Bill 6 (SB 6) rulemakings to offer workable refinements (including proposing and supporting a

minimum transmission rate).2 At this time, however, TIEC remains concerned that the overall

approach reflected in the proposal is not well-suited to the realities of industrial operations, both

current and future.

         While TIEC has sought to avoid rate classifications driven by end-use of electricity or

business sector, there are significant differences in the development patterns of traditional

industrial loads and the new computational proj ects. As compared to traditional industrial proj ects,

data center loads are generally larger, more modular, and more operationally homogenous. They

manufacturing facilities typically require highly specialized feedstocks, a long-term skilled

workforce (not just short-term construction), access to specific modes of transporting product to

global markets, and additional environmental specifications. These projects are developed often

over five-plus years and expanded over decades, representing massive, long-term investments that

                          II.     RESPONSES TO STAFF'S QUESTIONS

1.      Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
        be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
        different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

        Load size would be a reasonable, non-discriminatory basis for establishing a large load

minimum billing demand.          Specifically, TIEC recommends a threshold for the minimum

transmission rate of 300 MW or more of incremental load requested within any three-year period

at a single location. While TIEC believes Staff' s intent is for this rule to only apply to new or

expanded interconnections, TIEC would recommend making that clear in this rule, as well as in

the pending rule in Project No. 58481. Notably, the proposed definition of"large load customer"

in Proj ect No. 58481 is problematic because it keys in on the customer' s "total expected non-

coincident peak demand at a single site," which would subject an existing customer's entire load

to the minimum rate whenever any expansion pushes total site demand to 75 MW or above-even

ifthe incremental addition itselfis small. In particular, the rule should be clear that if a site pursues

an expansion, the pre-existing portion ofthe site will not be subject to the minimum demand charge

as a result of that expansion.

        To avoid this overbroad reading, we propose that the definition of Large Load Customer

in Project No. 58481 (which is used in this rulemaking) be revised to clarify that the 75 MW

threshold is measured against the incremental load being added, rather than the customer's total

existing site demand.    Correspondingly, TIEC' s related redlines in Attachment A to this rule

should be read to apply only to incremental load.

        As noted above, the impetus for this new minimum rate construct appears to be concerns

about the significant transmission needs for a high volume of "extra" large loads. It is not being

driven by the steady, incremental industrial development that the state has successfully managed

                                                   4
 for decades. In general, a 300 MW threshold appears to provide a reasonable distinction between

historical projects and these new "extra-fast and extra-large proj ects" that are driving the minimum

rate policy. Very few traditional industrial customers exceed 300 MW at a single location, and

those that do typically developed the projects in phases over many years that were each under 300

MW. TIEC acknowledges that it recommended a 250 MW threshold in prior comments on this

topic, which was based on the actual operational loads for legacy industrial businesses. However,

after further diligence TIEC has concluded that the interconnection requests/non-coincident peaks

are often slightly oversized for atl customers for contingency scenarios (this is discussed further

below). Recognizing this dynamic, TIEC is adjusting its recommendation to 300 MW and above

to provide an additional buffer.

       For the historical cadence of new sub-300 MW industrial loads, the existing

interconnection   framework-including        financial   security,   ramping    requirements,    and

contributions-in-aid-of-construction (CIAC)-has worked well for decades, allowing meaningful

protections against shifting costs to other customers without imposing unmanageable up-front

financial burdens on companies seeking to do business in Texas.

       Notably, however, a 300 MW threshold will still capture certain types of industrial

projects-including those that are critical to state and national priorities.     Specifically, LNG

facilities and semiconductor fabrication plants are still likely to be picked up by this threshold.

The state competes heavily to attract these businesses, which often represent tens of billions in

long-term investment. Hefty up-front minimum transmission rate requirements imposed before a

project is fully operational could be a major deterrent. Legislators have repeatedly raised concerns

about ensuring that requirements aimed at data centers do not stop traditional businesses from




                                                  5
 siting in Texas.3 Applying the same undifferentiated minimum billing demand requirements to

these industries will risk disadvantaging Texas when these customers are deciding where to locate

their next facility or whether or not to expand. The Commission should consider an exemption

process or alternative path for these types of projects.          Alternatively, while it is not TIEC' s

preferred approach, the Commission may ultimately need to consider distinguishing between

computational loads and traditional industrial loads if it seeks to pursue policies that are not

manageable for the industrial community. This is discussed further below.

        Finally, TIEC recognizes that there will be an incentive to "game" the threshold by

building, for example, 299.9 MW loads. TIEC believes this concern can be addressed without

abandoning a size-based threshold based on current development trends, where market demand is

predominantly for sites with 500, 1000, or 2000 MW of demand. Given that this emerging market

does not appear to be as cost-sensitive, it is likely that the demand for a larger site will outweigh

the cost consequences of exceeding the threshold for a minimum transmission rate. Further, the

2.      Should the large load minimum billing demand be: fixed for 20 years as proposed;
        reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or extended to a longer time period?

       A shorter, fixed term of approximately five years is appropriate for traditional industrial

customers, and any phase-down should be built around that shorter horizon rather than stretched

across twenty years. For the cadence and size oftraditional industrial growth, there is very limited

risk of any "stranded" facilities or cost-shifting.      Typically, any theoretically under-utilized

capacity on the system is either: (a) covered by existing CIAC and/or financial security

requirements, if the facilities are driven by the individual customer, or (b) fully utilized by other

customers within five years or less for more general system upgrades.

        The proposed rule would require a large load customer to begin 20 years of billing as soon

as service is available, regardless of whether the customer has energized or is using its full capacity.

While the rule does not address this, in otherjurisdictions these types of minimum rates have come

along with collateral/security requirements.      TIEC would expect the utilities to impose these

requirements ifthey are not addressed in the rule. The longer this minimum billing demand period

runs, the longer a customer' s collateral and security obligations must remain in place to support it,

and the amounts of security being held will be orders of magnitude higher than what utilities have




                                                   7

protection requires would increase collateral requirements and deter economic development. For

cost-sensitive traditional manufacturing customers, a 20-year minimum billing demand-paired

with the security and CIAC obligations under development in Project No. 58481-is simply

unworkable.

         Importantly, TIEC' s members make long-term investments and rarely shut them down

within decades of their construction. The infrastructure required for complex industrial facilities

is capital-intensive and site-specific, and it typically takes years to plan, permit, and construct.

Texas utilities have extensive experience in planning for and interacting with these customers.

Because of this, the risk that a traditional industrial load will fail to materialize or will abandon its

capacity after interconnecting is fundamentally different from the risk that the large load minimum

billing demand provisions appear to be designed to address. As noted above, based on historical

load growth, any theoretically underutilized system upgrades would likely be used by other

customers within a five-year growth period, and stakeholders have broadly agreed with that

timeframe.5 A minimum billing demand period that runs four times that length is not calibrated to

the actual risk presented by traditional industrial loads. A five-year term also gives ERCOT and

transmission proj ects recommended at the conclusion of a batch study.           The fundamental

distinction in transmission cost recovery is between costs dedicated to serving a specific customer

and costs that benefit the broader system.       Costs dedicated to a specific customer should be

recovered through a CIAC- a direct, upfront payment from that customer-rather than socialized

into transmission rates paid by all ratepayers. Only costs that serve the system as a whole belong

in rates. Broadening the interconnection-cost definition to sweep in system upgrades identified by

both existing and new customers onto individual new customers.

through the Batch process along with a // existing load. The system must be designed and built to

serve all customers, and if existing customers did not exist, a different set of upgrades would be

identified. Further, it is impossible to identify which particular system upgrades are attributable

to an individual customer. Transmission planning studies model all existing and planned load

under various contingencies, and identified upgrades may be driven by locational constraints and

specific contingency assumptions rather than the general usage of a particular customer or group

of customers. It is not possible to isolate what portion of the resulting transmission investment is

"caused" by any single customer or individual load. It is therefore inappropriate-and technically

infeasible-to treat batch-study-driven proj ect costs as interconnection costs that can be directly

assigned to a specific customer.

        The interaction between the financial security requirements in Project No. 58481 and the

        Under Project No. 58481, a large load customer must post $50,000 per MW at the

intermediate agreement stage, and post additional security for actual identified system upgrades

when signing an interconnection agreement.       This is in addition to either directly paying or

financially securing CIAC for all direct interconnection costs. As the rule in P. 58481 is currently

revenue commitments for large loads have paired those commitments with financial security that

       As explained above and in prior comments, the Commission' s ultimate decisions in this

project must be tethered to cost-causation. This is a fundamental tenet of regulated ratemaking

and is necessary to (a) incentivize those who are able to respond to rates/prices to moderate their

use ofthe transmission system during periods of system stress, and (b) to fairly reflect each class' s

contribution to periods of demand that drive the need for additional infrastructure.

         Applying a new rate construct to usage that already occurred-before the rules vvere

changed-deprives customers of any ability to modify their behavior to manage their costs. This

raises a basic fairness problem. This is especially acute for customers that actively managed their

usage under the prior framework. While the majority of TIEC's members are high-load factor

customers who either do not respond or only respond to 4CP around the margins, these savings

can still be meaningful for business customers and assessing transmission charges based on 12CP

demand that occurred before a 12CP regime had been adopted will impose sudden, significant cost

increases for responsive customers.

over a reasonable period, giving customers time to adjust before being held to the new framework.

Second, it could wait until 2027 usage data is available, so the new rate structure applies only

prospectively-based on actual usage under the new rules, not usage that predates them. Either

approach avoids the fairness problem of reaching back to penalize past behavior and ensures that

customers are measured against a framework in which they had the opportunity to respond.

        ramp/energization timelines should be equitably balanced between large customers
        and their utilities.

        In recent interim transmission rate updates, transmission utilities have proposed to place
transmission investment in rates before it is actually energized and serving customers.       This
creates two issues. First, investment that is not actually in operation is not "used and useful,"
which is a statutory prerequisite for an investment being placed in customer rates. Second, with
the potential for massive transmission build-out based on pending large customer interconnections

risk that other existing utility customers will pay for a significant portion of these while new large
loads are still under construction.

should be covered by the financial security requirements under P. 58481, (b) and utilities should
not be permitted to put costs of transmission investment into rates until the assets are actually
energized and serving customers. To provide clarity on this issue, the Commission should add the
following sentence to draft 16 TAC § 25.192(j)(2): "Onlv transmission facilities that have been
interconnected, energized, and are presently used and useful for providing utility service may be
included in an interim update under this section."

rates.   In § 25. 193(e) of the proposed rule, language was added allowing "projected" billing
